Players choose a scientific objective and orbit, select hardware within mass and budget limits, and physically assemble a probe while floating in microgravity. After verification and deployment through a science airlock, they manage observations, battery power, storage and communications.

details:
APOGEE is a first-person educational game set aboard a fictional lunar research station. Players design a mission, assemble a probe and operate it after deployment.

The player selects a scientific objective: terrain mapping, mineral signatures or a polar hydrogen survey. They then choose an orbit and five hardware categories: scientific instrument, power system, recorder, communications and transfer service. Mass, budget and transfer capability constrain the design.

Inside the station, players float in microgravity, retrieve components and install them in the laboratory. After completing acceptance checks, they deploy the assembled vehicle through a science airlock. The same hardware leaves the station, making the connection between design choices and the spacecraft visible.

During operations, OBSERVE records data, SUN POINT charges the battery and TRANSMIT returns observations to the station. Eclipse, energy reserves, recorder capacity, temperature and radio contact affect mission performance. Live feedback shows progress, waiting estimates, problems and the next action. The final report explains how the configuration and operating decisions affected scientific return.

The project uses Godot 4.7.2, GDScript and shaders and runs as a Windows desktop application. Features include procedural station geometry, six-axis movement, floating cargo, physical assembly, interactive hatches, an airlock sequence and save/load.

NASA lunar constants support simplified orbital calculations, while LRO imagery provides the Moon’s appearance. NASA mission-design resources informed the requirements, verification and operations workflow. Hardware specifications, prices, science units and station automation are fictional teaching assumptions. The game is not a validated flight simulator.

The intended benefit is to help students connect scientific objectives with engineering decisions and understand trade-offs between mass, cost, energy, storage and communications. Educational effectiveness has not yet been measured through classroom studies. Software verification includes 67 mission-model checks, 15 operations-feedback checks and a complete rendered gameplay scenario.

OpenAI Codex assisted with brainstorming, research, implementation, procedural graphics, debugging, automated checks, documentation and presentation preparation. The project lead defined the direction, tested gameplay and requested revisions. AI assistance and external assets are acknowledged in the source headers, README, NOTICE and SOURCES.md.
